newsitem.title: USA: White House, Congress optimistic on budget talks.
newsitem.headline: White House, Congress optimistic on budget talks.

text.p: The White House and members of Congress expressed optimism Friday that agreement could be reached soon on money to run the government when the new fiscal year starts Tuesday, but thorny issues were unresolved.

Working nearly around the clock Thursday and into Friday, negotiators talked their way through a more-than-2,000-page appropriations bill intended to fund everything from the Pentagon to the National Zoo. The talks broke off at 4 a.m. EDT and resumed a few hours later.
"We're getting there slowly, bit by bit, step by step," White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta said after the morning session.

Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, Democrat of South Dakota, said he felt time constraints would force Congress to act on a short-term spending bill soon to avoid any chance the government might be forced to close by a lack of funds.

But his Republican counterpart, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi, all but ruled out the idea, questioning Democratic motives in the talks. "I am very suspicious about some of the things I have seen. I mean, the way they negotiate there seems to be no end to it," he said.

Called an omnibus spending bill, it would cover the most costly government activities -- defence, education, labour, environmental protection, national parks, the White House, the Treasury, foreign aid, law enforcement and a host of others. Unless the money is approved for 1997, these agencies could be forced to close as they did twice last winter when a budget showdown led to a lapse in funding.

Polls show the public blamed last winter's partial closures on Republican congressional leaders and their "shutdown strategy" designed to force President Clinton to accept deep cuts in domestic spending.

Speaking to reporters, Daschle identified several issues including immigration reform, protection for physician communications with patients and a ban on gun ownership by convicted spouse abusers as important issues that remain.

These and the politically volatile issue of U.S. aid to international family planning agencies that use non-U.S. funds for abortion services will probably be left for negotiations at the highest levels in Congress and the White House.

Lott said Republican lawmakers were concerned the party had given the administration too much of what it wanted in agreeing to grant about $6.5 billion in extra spending for education, anti-terrorism and anti-drug efforts.
The money for these programmes would be raised by selling the wireless communications spectrum, raising thrift deposit insurance reserves and selling oil from the strategic petroleum reserve.

Senate Appropriations Committee Chairman Mark Hatfield, R-Oregon, said up to $1 billion in Pentagon money could be shifted to fight terrorism. About $300 million to $400 million of that would directly involve military programmes.
